question: Can a molecular-property GNN be competitive while exposing chemically useful signals at the atom, bond, fragment, and fragment-connection levels, including for salts and complexes?

key_findings.claim: FragNet constructs four coupled molecular graphs so learned bond and fragment-connection representations can condition atom- and fragment-level message passing.
key_findings.evidence: Bonds become nodes in a bond graph, BRICS substructures become fragment nodes, connections become nodes in a fourth graph, and lower-level learned features initialize the next graph's edges or nodes.

key_findings.claim: Virtual fragment connections let information pass between components without covalent bonds, a design aimed at salts, complexes, and ionic liquids.
key_findings.evidence: The construction links fragments across disconnected substructures and treats the links as possible non-covalent interactions; the fragment-connection graph then reasons over these links.

key_findings.claim: On seven MoleculeNet tasks with scaffold splits, FragNet is broadly competitive but not uniformly best.
key_findings.evidence: It reports the best listed ESOL, ClinTox, Sider, and Tox21 values, while SimSGT is better on LIPO and CEP; most comparison numbers were imported from prior work rather than generated in a single controlled rerun.

key_findings.claim: Fragment masking supplies a directional prediction-difference score that is more intervention-like than raw attention, although it is still a model-internal counterfactual.
key_findings.evidence: The contribution is the unmasked prediction minus the prediction after excluding a fragment's node features; positive and negative values are interpreted as property-increasing and property-decreasing effects.

key_findings.claim: The case studies find atom, bond, fragment, and connection patterns that the authors relate to known solubility, lipophilicity, and drug-response chemistry.
key_findings.evidence: Examples emphasize charged nitrogen, chloride, ether oxygen, aromatic systems, carbonyls, and polar fragment connections; aggregation is restricted to low-error predictions before ranking recurring substructures.

key_findings.claim: A small DFT comparison offers partial external support for solubility explanations, not a general validation of explanation faithfulness.
key_findings.evidence: For 16 selected molecules, fragment non-polar-to-polar electrostatic-surface ratios tend to align with negative contribution scores, especially for hydrophobic molecules; no causal ground-truth attribution benchmark is provided.

key_findings.claim: Error-stratified analysis identifies sodium-containing compounds as a concrete coverage failure.
key_findings.evidence: Sodium appears in 5.90% of the high-error group and none of the low-error group, motivating targeted data or representation improvements.

method.core_idea: Build an interpretable hierarchy of attention-based molecular graphs and expose both attention weights and fragment-masking prediction differences.
method.mechanism: A bond graph learns edge information for the atom graph; atom embeddings are summed into BRICS fragments; a fragment-connection graph learns edge information for the fragment graph; atom- and fragment-pooled representations are concatenated for prediction.
assumptions: BRICS fragments correspond to chemically meaningful explanatory units.
Virtual all-to-all links between disconnected components usefully proxy non-covalent relationships.
Attention magnitudes contain explanatory information despite not being causal attributions.
Masking a fragment without retraining produces a meaningful local counterfactual.
Scaffold-split MoleculeNet tasks and three seeds are adequate for the reported performance comparison.

techniques.role: Represents atoms, bonds, fragments, and fragment connections in coupled message-passing graphs.
Connects non-covalently bonded molecular components for salts and complexes.
Passes learned lower-level bond and atom features into higher-level graphs.
Measures the prediction change after removing a fragment's features.
Aggregates attention only on accurately predicted examples and separately mines high-error fragments.

evaluations.setting: Four regression and three classification MoleculeNet tasks under scaffold splits, three random seeds.
evaluations.metric: RMSE for regression and ROC-AUC for classification.
evaluations.result: Competitive with the listed pretrained molecular models, leading several tasks but trailing SimSGT on LIPO and CEP.
evaluations.baseline: ContextPred, AttrMask, JOAO, GraphMVP, Mole-BERT, SimSGT, and related methods.

evaluations.setting: Solubility, lipophilicity, and cancer-drug-response interpretation case studies.
evaluations.metric: Atom/bond/fragment/connection attention and fragment-masking contribution, aggregated over low-error examples.
evaluations.result: High-ranked groups are qualitatively connected to familiar polarity, hydrogen-bonding, steric, and aromatic effects.
evaluations.baseline: Known chemical heuristics and within-model low- versus high-contribution fragments.

evaluations.setting: Sixteen selected solubility molecules with DFT electrostatic surfaces.
evaluations.metric: Fragment non-polar/polar surface ratio versus FragNet contribution.
evaluations.result: Expected negative contribution trend is most visible for strongly hydrophobic molecules.

evaluations.setting: Top 20% highest-error solubility predictions versus predictions with error below 0.1.
evaluations.metric: Fragment frequency, mean error, attention, and contribution.
evaluations.result: Sodium is exclusive to the high-error group; several common fragments occur in both groups.

limitations: Attention weights are treated as explanations without causal faithfulness tests.
Masking can move a molecule off the learned data manifold and interactions make per-fragment effects non-additive.
The DFT comparison covers only 16 selected molecules and a polarity proxy, not all tasks or explanation levels.
Most baseline values are taken from another reference rather than rerun under one implementation and tuning budget.
BRICS fixes the explanatory vocabulary and may split or merge units differently from the mechanism of a property.
The public benchmarks plus a constructed PNNL solubility set do not establish prospective drug-design value.
Virtual connections encode possible interaction channels without distances, poses, or explicit physical energies.
failure_modes: Unseen ions or rare fragment types, exemplified by sodium, can yield large errors despite interpretable-looking weights.
Attention can be chemically plausible while not being necessary for the prediction.
Fragment masking can attribute correlated context to the removed fragment.
All-to-all virtual links may dilute or invent interactions between disconnected components.
A model may rank helpful fragments locally yet fail when proposed fragments are recombined into a new molecule.
reusable_insights: Pair performance benchmarking with error-conditioned explanation analysis so incorrect predictions are not rationalized as successes.
Expose representation failures as fragment-level coverage tables, which directly suggest targeted data acquisition.
Use multiple explanation views, but distinguish descriptive attention from intervention-based masking.
Represent disconnected molecular components explicitly when the task includes salts or complexes.
open_questions: Do masking scores recover causal substructures under controlled ground-truth molecular tasks?
How stable are explanations across seeds, scaffold splits, fragmentation schemes, and conformers?
Can interaction-aware Shapley or conditional masking replace independent fragment ablation at usable cost?
Do virtual fragment connections improve prospective salt and ionic-liquid prediction beyond atom-graph baselines?
Can uncertainty and out-of-distribution scores flag rare-fragment failures before interpretation?
Does explanation-guided molecule editing improve measured properties in a closed-loop experiment?

competitive_landscape.title: MoleculeNet: A Benchmark for Molecular Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: MoleculeNet standardizes datasets, splits, and metrics and shows the limits of learned molecular representations; FragNet uses a subset of those tasks to test an explicitly multilevel interpretable architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Analyzing Learned Molecular Representations for Property Prediction
competitive_landscape.difference: The D-MPNN study emphasizes broad public and proprietary predictive benchmarking; FragNet adds fragment hierarchies, virtual inter-fragment links, and explanation outputs but evaluates fewer endpoints.

competitive_landscape.title: GNNExplainer: Generating Explanations for Graph Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: GNNExplainer learns compact subgraph and feature masks for instance-level explanations across GNNs; FragNet builds chemically named explanatory levels into the predictor and reports attention plus direct fragment ablations.

competitive_landscape.title: Pre-training Molecular Graph Representation with 3D Geometry
competitive_landscape.difference: GraphMVP transfers 3D geometric information into a 2D molecular encoder for predictive accuracy; FragNet prioritizes interpretable 2D fragment structure and disconnected-component reasoning without explicit 3D pretraining.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: FragNet is the first single GNN framework to attend simultaneously to atoms, bonds, fragments, and fragment connections and to pass messages between non-covalently bonded fragments.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The architecture explicitly realizes the four graph levels, reports competitive MoleculeNet results, and demonstrates attention, masking, DFT, and error-stratified analyses.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The representation and UI-facing explanation stack is a useful systems contribution. The strongest novelty is multilevel fragment-connection reasoning; the evidence does not establish that its attention explanations are faithful or that explanation-guided design works prospectively.

reviewer_notes: Read all 37 extracted pages, including methods, seven benchmark tasks, interpretation case studies, DFT comparison, failure analysis, supplementary training details, and references. Current primary competitor records were checked on arXiv and the ACS publisher page on 2026-08-23.
